title: Reverse Linked List
directAnswer: Walk the list once, flipping each node's next pointer to point backwards. Keep three references — prev, curr, next — and at every step save curr.next, repoint curr.next to prev, then slide prev and curr forward by one. Return prev (the new head). O(n) time, O(1) space iteratively; the recursive version is the same idea but O(n) stack space.

remember.formula:
prev = None
curr = head
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next   # save before you overwrite
    curr.next = prev  # flip the link
    prev = curr       # advance prev
    curr = nxt        # advance curr
return prev
rules: Save `curr.next` into a temp **before** you overwrite it — otherwise you lose the rest of the list.
Return **prev**, not curr. When the loop ends `curr` is null and `prev` is the new head.
Initialise `prev = null`, so the old head's `next` becomes null and correctly terminates the reversed list.
The order inside the loop is fixed: save next → flip → advance prev → advance curr. Reordering breaks it.
Recursive version: recurse to the tail, then `head.next.next = head; head.next = null` on the way back up.
whenToUse: You must physically reverse a singly linked list or a sub-segment of one
A larger problem needs a reversed second half (Reorder List, Palindrome Linked List)
Reversing in groups of k (Reverse Nodes in k-Group) — same flip, bounded window
Any time you need to traverse a singly linked list backwards without extra memory
antiSignals: You only need to *read* the list backwards once → push to a stack or use recursion's call stack
It's a doubly linked list → swapping prev/next pointers per node is the natural move
You must not mutate the input → build a new reversed list instead of in-place flipping
remember.takeaway: The three-pointer flip is the single most reused linked-list primitive in interviews. Master `prev/curr/next` here and you get Reorder List, Palindrome Linked List, and Reverse Nodes in k-Group almost for free.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manipulate pointers in place without losing the list — specifically whether you save the next node before overwriting the current node's link.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Overwriting curr.next before saving it (losing the rest of the list), or returning the original head / curr instead of prev.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer both iterative O(1)-space and recursive solutions, explain why prev starts as null, and connect the flip to Reorder List and Reverse k-Group.

problemStatement:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return *the reversed list's head*.

Each node holds an integer `val` and a `next` pointer. After reversing, the node that was last should be the head, and the original head should point to `null`.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]
Follow up: can you do it both iteratively and recursively?
understanding: We reverse the direction of every `next` pointer in place. No new nodes are created and no values are copied — only the links between existing nodes change. The empty list and a single node are valid inputs that should be returned unchanged.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I mutate the existing nodes, or must I build a new list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In-place mutation is expected here and gives O(1) space. If mutation were forbidden, I'd allocate a fresh reversed copy at O(n) space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return for an empty list or a single node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return the head unchanged. The iterative loop handles both naturally — it just never executes or executes once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want iterative, recursive, or both?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll lead with the iterative O(1)-space version since it's the production-safe one, then show the recursive version for the follow-up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there duplicate values or a cycle?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Values may repeat but that's irrelevant — we move pointers, not values. The input is a proper acyclic list, so no cycle handling is needed.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Iterative three-pointer flip is the default; recurse only if asked or if the call stack is acceptable.

approaches.name: Iterative — Three-Pointer Flip (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. It's the production-safe answer: O(1) space and no stack-overflow risk on long lists.
hints: To reverse a singly linked list you have to flip each next pointer. But the moment you do curr.next = prev, you've lost the link to the rest of the list. How do you avoid that?
Keep three references: prev (the node behind you, initially null), curr (the node you're flipping), and a temp for curr.next saved before you overwrite it.
Loop while curr != null: save nxt = curr.next, set curr.next = prev, then advance prev = curr and curr = nxt. When curr is null, prev is the new head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly one pass: each node is visited once and does O(1) pointer work. No auxiliary data structure, so space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
We rebuild the list's links one node at a time, dragging a `prev` pointer behind us. At each node we redirect its `next` to point at the node we just came from.

**Why we need three pointers.** A singly linked list only lets you go forward. The instant you execute `curr.next = prev`, the original forward link is gone — so before that line you must stash it in a temporary `nxt`. The three roles are: `prev` is everything already reversed, `curr` is the node being flipped right now, and `nxt` is the untouched remainder. Lose any one of them and you either corrupt the list or strand half of it.

**Why prev starts as null.** The original head becomes the new tail, and a tail's `next` must be `null`. By initialising `prev = null`, the very first flip sets `head.next = null` for free, correctly terminating the reversed list.

**Why the four lines are order-sensitive.** Save → flip → advance prev → advance curr. If you advance `curr` before flipping, you flip the wrong node. If you flip before saving `nxt`, you lose the rest of the list. The sequence is a tiny state machine and every step depends on the previous one.

**Where we end up.** The loop continues until `curr` walks off the end and becomes `null`. At that exact moment `prev` is sitting on the last real node — which is the new head — so we return `prev`. Returning `curr` (null) or the original `head` is the classic off-by-one bug.
approaches.insight: The whole trick is a sliding window of two adjacent nodes (`prev`, `curr`) plus a one-node lookahead (`nxt`). Once you internalise 'save the link you're about to destroy', every in-place linked-list rewrite — partial reversal, k-group reversal, reorder — becomes the same muscle memory.

approaches.name: Recursive — Flip on the Way Back Up
approaches.whenToMention: Bring it up for the explicit 'can you do it recursively?' follow-up, but note the O(n) stack cost on long lists.
hints: Imagine the list is already reversed from the second node onward. What single pair of pointer assignments fixes up the first node?
Recurse to the end first. The base case (null or single node) returns itself as the new head and bubbles that head back up unchanged.
On the way back, head.next is the node right after head. Set head.next.next = head to make it point back, then head.next = null so head becomes the new tail.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n nodes triggers one recursive call doing O(1) work → O(n) time. The recursion depth equals the list length, so the call stack is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
We let recursion carry us to the tail, then fix one link per frame as the stack unwinds.

**The recursive leap of faith.** Assume `reverseList(head.next)` already fully reverses everything *after* `head` and hands back the new head of that reversed sublist. That new head never changes again — we just thread it straight back up through every return. Our only job at this frame is to attach `head` onto the *end* of that reversed sublist.

**The two magic lines.** After the recursive call, `head.next` still points at the node that is now the *tail* of the reversed portion. So `head.next.next = head` makes that tail point back to `head`, splicing `head` on as the new last node. Then `head.next = null` severs `head`'s old forward link so it terminates the list correctly. Skip the second line and you create a two-node cycle between `head` and its neighbour.

**Base case.** When `head` is `null` (empty list) or `head.next` is `null` (single node / the original tail), there's nothing to flip, so we return `head` as the new head. This is the value that propagates unchanged all the way back to the top-level caller.

**Why it costs O(n) space.** There's no loop; the work lives in n stacked frames. For the 5000-node constraint here that's fine, but on a million-node list it would overflow the stack — which is exactly why the iterative version is the safer default to lead with.
approaches.insight: Recursion reverses the list 'from the back': the deepest frame establishes the new head, and each shallower frame welds one more node onto the growing tail. It's elegant but trades the iterative version's O(1) space for O(n) stack — a trade worth naming out loud.

dryRun.intro: Calls descend to the tail; the fixes happen as the stack unwinds back up.

steps.action: 3.next is null → base case, return 3 as newHead

code.python:
def reverseList(self, head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = self.reverseList(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

java.explanation: Base case: empty list or last node — it's already the new head, return it as-is.
Reverse the rest first; newHead is the deepest node and is threaded back up unchanged.
The node after head is now the tail of the reversed part — point it back to head.
Sever head's old forward link so it terminates the list; omit this and you create a cycle.

python.line: if head is None or head.next is None:
python.explanation: Base case stops the recursion and seeds the new head.
Recurse to the tail; new_head propagates up unchanged.
Make the next node point back to head.
Break head's forward link to avoid a 2-node cycle.

pitfalls: Forgetting head.next = null — leaves a cycle between the last two nodes.
Returning head instead of the bubbled-up newHead.
Ignoring stack depth — O(n) frames can overflow on very long lists.

commonMistakes: Overwriting curr.next before saving it in a temporary — the rest of the list is lost.
Returning the original head or curr (null) instead of prev.
In the recursive version, forgetting head.next = null and creating a cycle.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Flipping before saving the next pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Once curr.next = prev runs, the original forward link is gone. You must stash it first or you can never reach the rest of the list.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the wrong node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When the loop exits, curr is null and head points to null (it's the new tail). Only prev holds the new head.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = prev
    prev = curr
    curr = nxt
return head   # head is now the tail!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = prev
    prev = curr
    curr = nxt
return prev

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursive cycle from a missing null assignment
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After head.next.next = head, the two nodes point at each other. Without head.next = null you've built an infinite 2-node loop.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
new_head = self.reverseList(head.next)
head.next.next = head
# missing head.next = None -> cycle
return new_head
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
new_head = self.reverseList(head.next)
head.next.next = head
head.next = None
return new_head

patternNote: Canonical in-place pointer reversal. The prev/curr/next flip is the atomic operation behind Reverse Linked List II, Reverse Nodes in k-Group, Palindrome Linked List, and Reorder List. Recognise it whenever you must change link direction without extra memory.
